modules.title: Neighborhood Investigation
modules.mission: The youth advisory team has been asked to study Riverbend, one neighborhood in our fictional county. Look at how the place is set up, not at blaming the people who live there. Find the conditions that shape health, who is affected, what the community already does well, and where $1 million can help most.

profiles.name: Riverbend
facts: Most errands need a car; the bus is infrequent.
The only full grocery store and the main clinic are across the highway.
Strengths: a volunteer-run neighborhood association, community garden, and a park walking loop.

profiles.name: Eastgate
facts: A busy highway runs beside many homes (noise and traffic air pollution concerns).
Residents report housing quality concerns such as mold and heating problems.
Strengths: active faith and youth groups and strong neighbor networks.

profiles.name: Pine Ridge County
facts: Services are spread out; travel to care can take a long time.
Internet is unreliable, which limits online appointments and information.
Strengths: dependable volunteer groups and a close-knit community.

spots.info: The bus comes about once an hour on weekdays and does not run on Sundays. A trip to the grocery store takes about 55 minutes with one transfer.
The only full grocery store is about 5 miles away on the far side of the highway. By car it is about 10 minutes; there is no sidewalk route.
Open weekdays 9 a.m.-4 p.m. and about 6 miles away. Routine appointments can take a few weeks to schedule. Many families have only one car.
Within walking distance. It stocks snacks, drinks and few fresh items.
A well-kept park with a walking loop. A volunteer walking club meets there on weekends.
Volunteers run a monthly food pantry, a ride-share board and weekly neighbor gatherings.
A small garden maintained by volunteers. Produce is shared with neighbors during the growing season.
Within walking distance for many students. After-school clubs are offered, and a school bus serves children who live farther away.

budgetOptions.t: Add weekday evening and Sunday bus service with a direct highway-crossing route
budgetOptions.note: Targets: car dependence, reaching grocery and clinic

budgetOptions.t: Run a mobile clinic that visits the neighborhood three days a week
Start a weekly farmers market with a produce delivery option for older adults
Build safe sidewalks and a crosswalk from the neighborhood to the school and park
Add evening activity programs at the park and association hall
Build a new full-service hospital in Riverbend
Buy billboards telling residents to eat healthier and see a doctor
budgetOptions.note: Awareness only; no change in access

data.note: Classroom case based on the community case files. Numbers are illustrative.

units.title: Name the condition
units.prompt: Each card is evidence from Riverbend. Choose the type of community condition (determinant) it shows best.

The clinic is open weekdays 9-4 and routine visits take weeks to schedule.

units.prompt: Select every statement that describes an environmental or systemic influence on Riverbend residents' health. Do not select statements that only describe an individual's own decision.

options.t: The bus does not run on Sundays, so some residents cannot reach the store or clinic.
A resident decides to skip breakfast on school mornings.
There is no sidewalk route across the highway to the grocery store.
A teen chooses to stay up late playing video games.
Routine clinic appointments take weeks to schedule.

units.prompt: Claim: "Trips to healthy food and health care take a long time without a car in Riverbend." On the map, select ONLY the places whose evidence directly supports this claim. Then select the groups most likely to be affected.

units.prompt: Choose the claim that best fits the Riverbend evidence, then the reason that best supports it.

Because Riverbend is car-dependent, its residents will all develop chronic disease.

options.t: Transportation, food and clinic access overlap, and the hall, garden and park already help neighbors.
People who live far from stores do not care about health.

The corner store is the only evidence needed.

modules.title: Public Health Operations Center
modules.mission: Reports of stomach illness are arriving after a neighborhood picnic. Your team helps the county health department decide what the data can and cannot tell us, and what each level of government does. Compare who ate what before you decide what caused the illness.

timeline.note: Maple Street picnic, about 60 people attend. Food sits on tables in warm sun for several hours.
First reports: stomach pain, vomiting. Two people visit urgent care.
A school nurse notices several absent students and reports it to the county health department.
Health department staff call attendees to ask who is ill and what they ate.

data.note: Fictional outbreak created for this assessment. No real people, place or agency.

units.title: Individual care or population protection?
units.prompt: Decide whether each action is mainly healthcare for one person, mainly public health for a population, or both. Remember that healthcare also includes prevention and public health also responds to existing threats.

rows.t: A doctor treats one student's ear infection.
A county program tracks flu cases in all schools to spot a spike.
A clinic gives a student a routine vaccine at a check-up, which also adds to community protection.
A health inspector investigates a restaurant after several people become ill.
A provider screens a teen for high blood pressure at an annual visit.

units.title: Who ate what?
units.prompt: Use the exposure table in the Operations Center. Of the people who ate chicken salad, what percent became ill? Of those who did NOT eat it, what percent became ill? Then choose the best conclusion.

fields.label: Percent ill among people who ate chicken salad
Percent ill among people who did not eat chicken salad
Best conclusion

options.t: Chicken salad is the leading suspect, but more evidence is needed before confirming the cause.
The chicken salad definitely caused the illness because the cluster happened after the picnic.
The lemonade is the leading suspect because it was the most-eaten item.
No food can be linked, so the data are useless.

units.title: Agent, host, environment, and next steps
units.prompt: First, match each piece of the picnic scenario to the agent-host-environment triangle. Then put the investigation steps in the order a health department would usually do them.

rows.t: A disease-causing germ (such as a bacterium) that may be in the food
The people who ate at the picnic
Food sitting for hours on a table in warm sun

fields.label: Order the steps

items.t: Compare who ate what among ill and well people
Use findings to take action (for example remove the food and advise the public)
Collect and count the case reports (surveillance)
Test samples and inspect how food was prepared and stored
Interview ill and well attendees about what they ate

units.title: Prevent it, find it, reduce harm; and who does what
units.prompt: Classify each action by prevention level, then match each task to the organization that most commonly does it. (Responsibilities can vary by state and county, so choose the best typical match.)

rows.t: A school hosts a vaccination clinic before flu season.
A county offers blood-pressure screening at a community fair to find problems early.
A rehabilitation program helps people recover from a stroke and prevent complications.
Inspect local restaurant kitchens and run a neighborhood immunization clinic
Fund research into new treatments
Track diseases nationally and give outbreak guidance and support
Set and enforce air and water pollution standards

modules.title: Environmental Safety Lab
modules.mission: Your team helps a school and a community plan safe activities. Explore how hazard, exposure, intensity, duration and susceptibility change risk. Exploring is unlimited and ungraded; only a submitted answer uses an attempt. Good plans use layers of protection before, during and after an activity, name who decides, and say when to modify, pause or stop.

smoke.setup: The varsity soccer team has an outdoor practice this afternoon. The AirNow forecast for the field area is an AQI of 135 to 155 (the range crosses from "Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups" into "Unhealthy"). Two players have asthma.

options.t: Each player decides alone

noise.caution: This is an occupational recommended limit for a workday. It is not a guarantee that listening below it is risk-free, and it is not a guarantee of safety at any level for every person.

advisories.d: Germs (microbes) may be in the water. Boiling can make water safe for drinking and cooking, as the advisory instructs.
Chemicals or toxins may be in the water. Boiling will NOT remove them. Use bottled or other safe water for drinking and cooking as instructed.
Contact may be harmful. Do not drink, cook with, or wash with the tap water; use other safe water as instructed.

refs.t: AQI is a color-coded index of outdoor air quality. It is not a direct measure of any person's dose; breathing hard for longer or having asthma changes what you take in. (AirNow AQI basics)
UV Index 8-10 is Very High; 11+ is Extreme. Guidance: seek shade, cover up, wear a hat and sunglasses, and use SPF 30+ sunscreen reapplied about every 2 hours. (EPA UV Index scale)
Heat index is calculated for shade and light wind. Direct sun can raise the "feel" substantially. Heat risk also depends on activity, equipment and acclimatization. (National Weather Service)
NIOSH recommended exposure limit: 85 dBA for 8 hours, halving the time for every 3 dBA increase (occupational guidance). (CDC/NIOSH)

units.title: Risk vocabulary and time scales
units.prompt: Match each example to the risk idea it shows. Then decide whether each health effect is mainly short-term or long-term.

rows.t: Tiny smoke particles (PM2.5) or secondhand smoke in the air

units.title: Plan: soccer practice in smoke
units.prompt: Use the lab to build a plan for the soccer practice. A strong plan lowers exposure, protects sensitive players, checks conditions, names who decides, and says when to act.

units.title: Plan: lifeguard in high UV
units.prompt: Build a layered UV plan for the lifeguard. There is no exact "time until burn" for any one person, so plan for protection and monitoring, not a stopwatch.

units.title: Loud concerts and the time-limit chart
units.prompt: Use the noise chart in the lab. Each 3 dBA increase cuts the recommended time in half. Read or work out the answer, then choose the best conclusion.

fields.label: At 100 dBA, about how many minutes per day does the NIOSH recommended exposure limit allow?
A student attends a 100-dBA concert for 30 minutes without hearing protection. Best conclusion:

options.t: It is safe, because 30 minutes is much shorter than 8 hours.
It is over the occupational recommended time for that level, so protection, distance or shorter time would reduce the risk. Being under a limit would still not guarantee zero risk.
Only sounds above 120 dBA ever matter.
Any one loud event causes permanent hearing loss for everyone.

units.title: Plan: football practice in heat
units.prompt: Build a plan for the football practice. Include who decides and when to modify, pause or stop. The plan should rely on a written school heat plan and conditions, not one magic number.

units.title: Water advisory decisions
units.prompt: Match each situation to the best advisory type. Then answer the boiling question. Always follow the advisory your local officials issue.

rows.t: Tests found germs in the water supply. Officials say water is safe to drink after boiling.
A chemical spill reached the water system. Swallowing the water could be harmful.
Tap water could be harmful to drink and also to touch or bathe in.

fields.label: A family under a do-not-drink advisory for a chemical spill boils their tap water. What happens?

options.t: Boiling removes the chemicals, so the water is safe.
Boiling does not remove chemicals; they should use the safe water the advisory names, such as bottled water.
Boiling for ten minutes always makes any water safe.
Cooling it in the fridge first makes it safe.

modules.title: Health Data Observatory
modules.mission: The advisory team receives a small table comparing four fictional communities. Read the graphs and the table, make careful comparisons, and decide what the data can and cannot say. These numbers are fictional classroom data about community averages. They do not describe any real place or predict anything about an individual student.

rows.t: Riverview
East Junction
Pine Hills
Lakeview

units.prompt: Use the four charts or the table. Choose the community that shows the greatest need on these measures, then select every statement that the table supports.

fields.label: Community showing the greatest burden on all four measures

options.t: Riverview
East Junction

modules.title: Media and Source Studio
modules.mission: A sponsored post is going around the school. The advisory team decides how to read it and which sources to trust. Use Audience -> Emotion -> Message -> Action to see how it works, P.A.U.S.E. to question it, and STOP to pick useful information. A marketing technique does not automatically make a claim false; check the evidence.

post.note: Constructed classroom example. Not a real product, person or agency.
post.caption: Be the athlete you're meant to be! SparkUp Boost is all-natural, plant-powered energy that boosts your focus. Over 50,000 cans sold THIS WEEK. Only 2 hours left for 30% off with code MAYA30!

cues.note: Words that sound healthy do not tell you what is in the product or whether it is good for you.

cues.t: "Be the athlete you're meant to be"
cues.note: Links the product to who you want to be.
Popularity is not evidence that something works or is safe.
Time pressure discourages checking the evidence.
A trusted face is not the same as an independent source.

cues.t: "#sp" at the end of a hashtag list
cues.note: Clear sponsorship disclosure should be easy to notice and understand. "sp" is an abbreviation that many viewers will not recognize.
A personal code can pay or credit the influencer when you buy.
No study, amount or source is given for this claim.

references.title: Air Quality Index (AQI) Basics
references.claim: Six AQI categories and ranges: Good 0-50, Moderate 51-100, Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups 101-150, Unhealthy 151-200, Very Unhealthy 201-300, Hazardous 301+; higher AQI means greater health concern; sensitive groups affected first.

references.title: UV Index Scale
references.claim: UV Index 8-10 Very High and 11+ Extreme; protection includes shade, hat, sunglasses, protective clothing, SPF 30+ sunscreen reapplied about every 2 hours, and limiting midday sun. No individual burn clock is given or used.

references.title: Understand Noise Exposure
references.claim: NIOSH recommended exposure limit (REL) 85 dBA averaged over 8 hours with a 3 dBA exchange rate (time halves per 3 dBA). It is an occupational recommendation and not a guarantee of safety.

references.title: Heat information (Heat Index)
references.claim: Heat index categories (caution, extreme caution, danger, extreme danger) and that values are for shade and light wind; direct sun can add up to about 15 °F. Category edges differ slightly between excerpts, so tasks use only a value (98 °F) inside "extreme caution" under either edge and state no cancel threshold.

references.title: Drinking Water Advisories: An Overview
references.claim: Boil-water, do-not-drink and do-not-use advisories differ; boiling kills germs but does not remove chemicals; follow the advisory instructions.

references.title: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
references.claim: Material connections (such as payment or free products) should be disclosed clearly and conspicuously; abbreviations such as "sp" are not adequate disclosures.

steps: You are joining the county youth advisory team. Your job: investigate a fictional county, then present an evidence-based plan.
Click a glowing place on the county map to travel there. Each place has a mission, an investigation panel, and scored questions.
Exploring is free and unlimited. Only pressing Submit on a question uses an attempt, and every question gives you three submitted attempts.
Credit for a question: correct on attempt 1 = 100%, attempt 2 = 85%, attempt 3 = 75%, never correct = 0%.
You can use the keyboard (Tab, arrow keys, Enter, Space) for everything. Use the Motion toggle in the top bar to turn animations off.
